premise: A delivery rider realizes every address on today's route belongs to someone who died in the same building.

plan.series_logline: A delivery rider discovers that every address on their route belongs to a dead resident of the same building, forcing them to unravel a century‑old conspiracy while confronting their own mortality.
plan.promise: A tense, atmospheric mystery that blends supernatural intrigue with a deep exploration of grief, memory, and the hidden histories of urban spaces.

characters.name: Alex Mercer
characters.defining_facts: Late 20s, haunted by a childhood loss, works nights for a courier app
characters.arc: From detached courier to reluctant conduit between the living and the dead, Alex learns to accept mortality and becomes the key to resolving the century‑old mystery.

characters.name: Maya Patel
characters.defining_facts: Mid‑30s, skeptical, driven by a desire for truth, works for a local newspaper
characters.arc: Starts as a cynical reporter chasing a sensational story, discovers the supernatural reality, and ultimately becomes Alex’s confidante and partner in unraveling the conspiracy.

characters.name: Dr. Evelyn Lark
characters.defining_facts: Early 50s, specializes in urban legends, holds key records of the building’s past
characters.arc: Transitions from detached scholar to personally invested guardian of the building’s secrets, revealing the truth about the deaths.

characters.name: Detective Luis Reyes
characters.defining_facts: Late 40s, pragmatic, skeptical of the supernatural, assigned to the cold case unit
characters.arc: Moves from skeptic to believer, uses his investigative skills to protect Alex and help bring closure.

characters.name: The Whisper
characters.defining_facts: Former resident, died in a fire 120 years ago, possesses the ability to influence the living
characters.arc: From vengeful spirit seeking retribution to seeking redemption and closure, ultimately aiding Alex in resolving the cycle of deaths.

characters.name: Officer Chen
characters.defining_facts: Early 30s, supportive, part of the precinct
characters.arc: Provides logistical support and comic relief, grows to respect Alex’s mission.

episodes.title: Dead Drop
episodes.text:
Alex tightened the strap on his battered messenger bag as the rain began to drum against the city’s cracked sidewalks. The courier app blinked: 17 addresses, all in the same block, all on the same street—Avenue B. He’d been riding these routes for months, but today something felt off. He pulled a stack of envelopes from the bag, each stamped with a different name and a building number that matched the same old brick façade of the 1920s‑era complex that had stood since the city’s early boom. He’d seen the building before; its windows were all dark, its doors locked, but the sign still read “Building 17.”

His first drop was a small, unmarked parcel for a woman named Evelyn Lark, an art curator who lived on the fourth floor. The keyhole was a rusty old thing; he turned the key he’d been given by the dispatch office and slipped the parcel into the slot. A faint click echoed, and a cold draft rushed out. Alex felt a chill that had nothing to do with the weather.

When he walked back, the next address—Maya Patel, a local journalist—was already boarded up. He tried the door; it wouldn’t budge. He pressed his ear to the wood and heard a faint, almost inaudible sigh. He ran the rest of the route, dropping packages at empty doorways and boarded windows. Every address on the list was either locked or abandoned. He checked the delivery app: the names matched the building’s resident list, but the dates of death on the city records were all in 2023.

He stopped at the front door of the building, a heavy oak door with a brass plaque that read “Building 17.” He pressed his palm against it, and the plaque seemed to pulse faintly. He pulled his phone out and scrolled through the city’s public records. The list of residents matched the names on his packages, but each had a death certificate dated the same day—September 12, 2023. He stared at the screen, heart pounding. The app’s notification pinged: “Delivery completed.” He didn’t have time to read the message. He was already turning to leave.

As he rode away, the rain softened into mist. A sudden thought struck him: the delivery route, the names, the dates—all a pattern. He could not shake the feeling that the city’s bureaucracy had somehow been orchestrated to line up these deaths. He imagined the building’s empty rooms, the ghostly presence of those who had once lived there. He wondered if the route itself was a list of ghosts.

The last drop, a small box addressed to a man named Samuel Ortiz, was left at the back door of a unit that had been vacant for years. He pulled the box out of the slot, and the latch squealed. Inside, a folded newspaper clipping read: *“Building 17: A Legacy of Tragedy.”* He flipped it over, his breath catching on a headline: *“Unsolved Fire Claims 120 Lives.”* The photo under the headline showed the same building, but the basement was a dark void.

Alex’s phone buzzed. A message from Maya: *“I know the building. It’s not just a rumor. We need to talk.”* He stared at the screen, the image of the building reflected in the rain‑slick pavement. He felt the weight of the unanswered questions settle over him like a shroud. He pushed his bike into the rain, the city lights flickering behind him.

Is the delivery route a list of ghosts? The question hung in the air, as tangible as the mist that clung to the street.

episodes.title: Ghost in the Mailbox
episodes.text:
Alex rode the familiar loop of Avenue B, his ears tuned to the rhythm of the city and his eyes scanning the gray façades of Building 17. Each address he passed was a dead name, a hollow door that had seen no living breath since September 12, 2023. The first day he had stumbled upon a newspaper clipping in a package, a faded photograph of the 1923 fire that had gutted the third floor. The paper had been tucked inside a parcel for the 12th‑floor tenant, a man who had died that same day, and Alex had slipped it into the mailbox before the delivery was complete.

The second day, the same route felt heavier. As he slid the key into the lock of the sixth‑floor door, he saw a new envelope on the doorstep. It was a plain, cream‑colored envelope, no stamps, no return address, but a symbol pressed into the top corner: an inverted triangle. The envelope was thin, almost translucent, and inside lay a single sheet of paper, a newspaper clipping that Alex had never seen before. The headline read, “Mysterious Deaths Plague Building 17.” The article, dated 1925, recounted a series of unexplained deaths over a five‑year span, all occurring on the same day of the week, each leaving behind a cryptic mark on the building’s walls. The article mentioned that the deaths were never solved, that the city had quietly sealed the case, and that no one had dared to investigate further.

Alex turned the page. The photograph on the back showed a line of twelve shadows, each silhouette outlined in a faint, triangular shape. The caption read, “The Twelve: A Pattern, a Mystery.” The article ended with a chilling line: “Whoever left the marks knows more than they let on.”

He felt the weight of the paper settle in his pocket. The envelope had been left on the doorstep, a silent invitation. He pressed the symbol into his palm, feeling its slight give. The inverted triangle seemed to pulse with a faint heat, a reminder of the fire’s embers still alive in the building’s bones.

He pushed open the door to the seventh floor. The hallway was a ghost of its former self, the paint peeling, the light flickering. At the end of the corridor, a small mailbox sat beneath the old brass plaque that read “Building 17.” Alex slipped the envelope inside, the paper slipping through the slot as if it were a secret letter. He then took a photo of the mailbox with the symbol now etched on its surface and sent it to Maya Patel, the journalist who had called him after the first drop. Maya had been skeptical, but she was intrigued by the pattern she had found in her research—an odd cluster of deaths in a single building. She had hinted that the story was bigger than a single fire.

The phone buzzed in Alex’s pocket. Maya’s voice came through, hushed and urgent. “You’re not alone in this, Alex. Someone else is watching, watching us. Keep your eyes open.”

He turned back to the hallway, his heart racing. The hallway’s walls were lined with old photographs, each frame a ghost of a life once lived. He felt a cold draft brush against his cheek, as if the building itself were breathing. He heard a faint click behind him, the sound of a lock turning. He spun around, but the hallway was empty.

The last thing he saw was the symbol on the mailbox, now illuminated by a single flicker of light from the hallway’s broken bulb. He felt the weight of the paper in his pocket, the question hanging in the air: Who left the clues behind?

“Then why bring the folder?”

She opened it. Inside lay a photocopy of a 1925 newspaper column, its paper brittle at the fold. The article described an old rumor: every September 12, residents of Building 17 heard a bell from a floor where no bell was installed. The reporter had dismissed it as a children’s tale. In the margin, someone had drawn an inverted triangle.

“I found it while checking the fire coverage,” Maya said. “The clipping from your package is real. This one is in the library’s microfilm archive. I don’t believe in ghosts. I do believe someone has been planting the same mark in records for a hundred years.”

Alex told her about Evelyn’s appearance and the ledgers beneath the building. Maya’s skepticism hardened at the word “ghost,” but she didn’t leave. She compared the triangle on the article to the image on his screen, then turned the page over. A line of type had been hidden in the fold: “The names were entered before the doors were opened.”

“That could mean anything,” she said, though she photographed it before sliding the article back into its sleeve. “Tomorrow I’ll check the original issue and the building permits. If they match, I’ll come back.”

At the door she stopped. “One more thing. The 1925 column mentions a group portrait taken after the fire. The library catalog says the photograph was donated under the name Evelyn Lark.”

Maya hadn’t seen it. She was already turning the clipping over again, studying the triangle.

The fourth‑floor window of Building 17 stared back at him, its glass a dull mirror of the sky. He leaned in, breath fogging the pane, and saw a faint outline—a woman in a 1920s dress, her profile framed by a shadow that matched the inverted‑triangle mark from the 1925 clipping. He flicked his phone to Maya’s message: *Did you see her?* The text blinked in the dim kitchen light. Maya’s face, framed by a stack of microfilm, was tense. She had been skeptical, but her fingers trembled as she traced the triangle on the newspaper page.

He lifted the page. The ink was fresh; the triangle’s edges were cut cleanly, as if a hand had carved it. A whisper brushed his ear—low, almost a sigh. He turned, but the hallway was empty, save for the echo of his own footsteps.

In the lobby, Tomas the concierge offered a cup of coffee. His eyes flicked to Alex’s phone, where Maya’s new message pulsed: *The triangle isn’t just a symbol. It’s a promise. The dead will be free if you bring them peace.*

Alex stared at the coffee, then at the glass of the lobby. The ledger in his pocket felt heavier than ever, the names inside weightless and unresolved. He could deliver the packages and leave the dead in their sorrow, or follow the whisper and try to set them right.

He pressed the elevator button. The doors slid shut, and the hum of the machinery seemed to echo the whisper that had guided him.

*Can he trust a ghost?* The question hung in the air as the elevator descended, the ledger clutched tight in his hand, the promise of peace echoing in his mind.

episodes.title: Ashes of the Past
episodes.text:
Alex’s route on Avenue B had always felt ordinary—17 stops, a dozen coffee shops, a few broken streetlights. Today, the elevator doors of Building 17 hissed open to a dim stairwell that smelled of old paper and dust. He tucked his phone into his jacket and stepped onto the landing. The brass plaque reading “Building 17” glinted in the weak shaft of light.

He pulled the first package from the back of his bike, a small box with a faded logo. The door was boarded up; a rusted keyhole stared up at him. He tapped the lock with the tip of his bike, listening for a click that never came. On the sixth floor, the mailbox was still marked with the cream‑colored envelope he’d seen earlier that morning—a fresh inverted‑triangle symbol etched into the metal, as if someone had just carved it. Alex’s breath fogged in the cold air.

A whisper—soft, almost a sigh—seemed to curl around him, drifting toward the stairwell. He followed it, heart thudding, until the echo faded against the concrete wall. He was on the fourth floor now, the glass of the lobby reflecting his own face. A figure in a long coat stood behind the glass, eyes flickering in the dim light. Alex caught a glimpse of a woman who looked familiar; she was Evelyn Lark, the archivist who had once curated the building’s records. She turned, and for a moment he thought she was a projection.

“Alex,” she said, her voice low and steady. “You’re getting closer. The triangle isn’t a symbol of death—it’s a promise. The people who died on September 12, 2023, were bound to a secret that began with that fire in 1923. The ledger I showed you… it’s not just names. It’s a covenant.”

He swallowed. Evelyn slid a thin, leather‑bound book toward him. Inside, the pages were filled with entries dated every September 12 from 1925 to 1927, each name accompanied by an inverted‑triangle. The last page, dated 2023, had his own name written in a cramped hand, the triangle freshly inked beside it.

“Why me?” Alex whispered.

Evelyn’s eyes softened. “Because you’re the one who can bring them peace. The Whisper—if you trust me—has been waiting. He promised to help you.”

Alex felt the weight of the book, of the promise. He remembered the message from Maya, the journalist who had warned him of the triangle’s danger. Maya’s voice had been skeptical, but she had also shown him the microfilm copy of the 1925 column, the hidden note that read, *The names were entered before the doors were opened.*

The Whisper’s voice floated up the stairs, a murmur that seemed to come from the floorboards themselves. “Deliver the package,” it said, “and let the promise be fulfilled.”

Alex’s hand tightened on the book. The elevator’s doors opened onto the fifth floor. He stepped inside, the metal doors closing behind him with a soft click. The elevator’s lights flickered, then steadied, casting a pale glow over the cabin. He could hear the faint thud of something below, a heartbeat in the walls.

He pressed the button for the ground floor, the one that would bring him to the basement he had read about in the fire report. The elevator shuddered, then began its descent.

At the bottom, the air grew colder, the smell of wet stone and old timber. He saw a set of stairs leading down into darkness, the corridor lined with peeling wallpaper that bore the same inverted‑triangle pattern he’d seen on the ledger. He could feel the weight of the past pressing against him, a silent chorus of voices waiting for release.

Alex’s phone vibrated—Maya’s name flashing on the screen. She had sent a photo of a new clipping, dated 1925, with a fresh note that read, *What lies beneath the floorboards?*

He looked up at the dim light above, the triangle etched into the ceiling. The Whisper’s voice whispered again, “Answer the question, Alex.”

The elevator doors slid open, and he stepped into the darkness, the promise of the past calling him forward.

*What lies beneath the floorboards?*

episodes.text:
Maya spread the photocopies across the diner table, keeping one hand on the oldest page so the ceiling fan wouldn’t lift it. Alex had sent her a photograph from the archive: a ledger open to September 12, 1925. She had spent the afternoon comparing it with the newspaper microfilm and the city’s cold-case index.

“I found the files,” she said. “Not one case. A sequence.”

The first report described two residents found dead after the 1923 fire, their room locked from the inside. The next file, dated September 12, 1926, listed three more names from Building 17. A 1927 report added four. The causes were marked undetermined, then crossed out and reclassified as accidents. No suspect. No trial. Each file closed with the same phrase: no evidence of a common cause.

Maya tapped the margins. “Different investigators. Same correction in the same ink. Someone changed the classification after the reports were filed.”

Alex studied the names. Several appeared in the old ledger Evelyn had shown him. “Could the deaths be connected to the fire?”

“Maybe. But the dates don’t line up with the fire itself. They happen years later, always on September 12.” She slid over a grainy image of the 1925 article. The inverted triangle sat beside the final paragraph. “I still don’t know what the symbol means. I do know someone kept altering these records.”

She had expected Alex to tell her about another whisper or another impossible door. Instead, he told her what the Whisper had offered: help bringing the dead to peace, in exchange for Alex’s cooperation. Maya’s expression tightened.

“That’s not proof it can help,” she said. “And anyone who asks for your trust before explaining the price is asking you to take a risk.”

She gathered the pages and turned to the last file in the folder. It wasn’t from the 1920s. A fresh tab read BUILDING 17, SEPTEMBER 12, 2023. The public record listed the same date for every resident on Alex’s route. The attached investigator’s note was short: no common cause established; case closed.

“They closed seventeen deaths without naming a responsible party,” Maya said. “That’s not an answer.”

Alex looked again at the list. The names matched the entries he had delivered to. At the bottom, someone had added a line in pencil: MAYA PATEL—WITNESS, INTERVIEW PENDING.

Maya went still. “I’ve never been interviewed about Building 17.”

The folder’s cover bore a date-stamp from the city archive: received tomorrow.

Maya laid the cold-case photocopies across the lobby desk. The dates marched down the page: September 12, 1925; September 12, 1926; September 12, 1927. Beside each report, a clerk had typed “accidental death.” Beside each correction, someone had drawn a small inverted triangle.

“This isn’t a pattern until we know the files are genuine,” she said. “And it still doesn’t tell us who changed them.”

The caretaker, Hargrove, had been listening from the stairwell. He stepped into the lobby but kept his hands in his coat pockets. “You’re looking in the wrong records.”

Maya turned. “Then show me the right ones.”

Hargrove glanced at Alex. “You’ve already met the thing in this building. You know the dead aren’t just names on a page.”

“That isn’t evidence,” Maya said.

“No. It’s why I stayed.” He studied the photocopies without touching them. “For years the night staff told stories about a group that met here every September twelfth. They called themselves the Keepers. They believed the fire left something unfinished, and that remembering the dead kept it from spreading.”

Maya’s expression didn’t change. “You’re repeating a rumor.”

“I’m telling you what I heard. I never saw a meeting.” Hargrove reached into his coat and set a folded carbon copy on the desk. Its edges had yellowed; the heading read “Maintenance—September 1927.” The last lines listed a room inspection and three sets of initials. Under them sat the inverted triangle.

Maya took a photograph before opening the sheet. “Where did you get this?”

“Inside the old boiler log, when I started here. I put it back. I shouldn’t have kept a copy.”

The note beside the initials read: “Names entered before doors opened. Witness to be informed when the rider returns.”

Alex felt his throat tighten. That phrase had appeared on the 1925 clipping too. Maya compared the two photographs, then zoomed in on the carbon copy. The initials were blurred, but the paper bore a stamped archive number.

“This could still be fabricated,” she said. “I’ll check the number against the city catalog.”

Hargrove nodded. “That’s fair.” He started back toward the stairs, then stopped. “If the Keepers were real, they weren’t protecting the building. They were waiting for someone to finish the delivery.”

Maya looked up sharply. “What delivery?”

The caretaker’s face tightened. “I don’t know.”

She turned the copy over. In fresh pencil, beneath the archive stamp, someone had written her name: MAYA PATEL. The handwriting matched the note she’d found on the 1925 clipping.

episodes.title: The Skeptic
episodes.text:
Detective Luis Reyes let Maya finish laying out the photocopies before he touched any of them. The cold-case office smelled of burnt coffee and warm printer toner. Alex stood beside the table, trying not to look at the badge clipped to Reyes’s belt.

“You want me to connect three accidental deaths from the twenties to seventeen deaths in 2023,” Reyes said. “And the connection is a triangle?”

“The same date, the same building, the same mark,” Maya replied. “The old reports were changed after filing. We’re asking who changed them.”

Reyes turned to Alex. “And you think a ghost told you this?”

“I think the register had my name on it before I knew it existed.”

“That’s not evidence of a ghost.” Reyes tapped the photocopy of the 1927 maintenance log. “But this is evidence somebody handled the records. Where did you get it?”

“The caretaker found it inside an old boiler log. He says a group called the Keepers met in the building.”

Reyes gave Maya a look. “You believe him?”

“I believe this copy matches the archive stamp. I don’t know what the group believed.” She slid over the city’s 2023 case summaries. “These were all closed as unrelated. I checked the dates against the public death records myself.”

Reyes read the summary sheet, then compared its case numbers with the old maintenance record. One number had been typed over. Under the correction, a triangle showed through the paper. His skepticism didn’t disappear, but his attention sharpened.

“I can’t take an original out of evidence,” he said. “I can take a logged copy.” He made a photocopy, wrote the archive reference on an evidence-transfer slip, and signed it. “I’m checking whether the correction matches our case index. That’s all. No ghosts, no secret society.”

Maya nodded. “That’s all we’re asking.”

Reyes put the copy in a clear sleeve and slipped it into his coat pocket. He paused at the door. “If the records are real, someone wanted them read. That doesn’t mean the message is meant for you.”

“Or for you,” Maya said.

He gave no answer.

At home, Reyes laid the sleeve under his desk lamp. The typed-over case number looked ordinary from the front. He turned the sheet. Pressure marks from a page above had left faint writing in the paper, invisible until the light hit at an angle.

Three words emerged beneath his signature: “REYES—WITNESS NEXT.”

His phone was already in his hand. He sent Alex a photo of the copy, then typed: “I don’t believe your ghost story. But someone knew I’d take this home.”

The returned parcel waited on the lobby desk when Alex came back from his route. Dispatch had marked it undeliverable and sent it back to the building, though the label named no apartment—only “Building 17, care of the archive.”

No names appeared on the front, only a black border and a line: “Service held in the west lobby after the fire.”

The moment Alex read it, the archive vanished.

He stood in the lobby as it must have looked a century earlier. Smoke stained the ceiling. Wet coats crowded the walls. A closed coffin rested beneath the brass plaque, while mourners filed past carrying little numbered tags in their palms. No one spoke. At the back, a woman pressed a triangle into the damp plaster with her thumb.

Alex tried to move, but the scene held him. A boy beside the coffin looked up. Soot darkened one cheek. He held out a tag marked 17.

“They wrote us down before they opened the doors,” the boy said.

The present slammed back around Alex. The archive shelves stood where they had been. His hands were empty, but the brass tag lay on the floor beside the program. Its number had been scratched through and replaced with a name: Samuel Ortiz.

Alex photographed both pieces and called Maya. She answered from the records office, papers shuffling near the receiver.

“The date matches the fire,” he said. “The program says the funeral was held in the west lobby.”

“There was no west lobby on the public plans,” Maya replied. Her voice had lost its usual edge of certainty. “Send me the tag. I’ll check the original building permits. Don’t decide what it means yet.”

Alex looked at the parcel label again. The sender field was blank. Beneath it, a faded dispatch stamp read RETURNED: RECIPIENT NOT FOUND.

The elevator groaned overhead. From somewhere above came the measured sound of a funeral bell—three notes, then silence. Alex placed the tag beside the 1927 maintenance copy. The stamped number matched a mark on the plan’s hidden corridor.

He turned the program over. In pencil, someone had added one name beneath the date: Luis Reyes.

The bell rang once more, this time from inside the sealed wall.

Maya chose the café because its tables sat beside a broad front window. She wanted daylight, witnesses, and a quick way out. Between them lay photocopies: the old cold-case reports, the 1927 maintenance note, and Reyes’s image of the pressure marks on his logged copy.

Alex nodded. “I didn’t ask you to.”

She tapped the 1927 note. “The archive stamp checks out, but the copy could have been altered later. Reyes taking it home doesn’t prove who wrote the message.”

“He thought the same thing.”

“Hargrove says old staff told stories about a group called the Keepers.”

“Stories,” she repeated. “Did he ever see a meeting?”

“No.”

“The public plans don’t show a west lobby,” she said. “I can check the original permits and compare the archive copy. If the room existed, someone removed it from the official record.”

“And if it didn’t?”

“Then we find out who forged the program.” She photographed the page, careful not to take it from him. “Either way, I’m investigating.”

Maya gathered the photocopies. “I’ll check the permits. You tell me exactly what you saw, even if you think I won’t believe it.”

For once, Alex had no evidence to show her—only the empty reflection and the certainty that the boy had been looking straight at him.

Alex knocked. The door opened onto a narrow office lined with books and archive boxes. No one stood inside. On the desk, a gray ledger lay open beneath a paperweight. Its cover bore the inverted triangle.

Maya stopped at the threshold. “Was someone just here?”

Alex didn’t answer. In the dark window behind the desk, he saw Evelyn Lark’s reflection. She wore the same cardigan from the archive; her face was pale, the fourth-floor corridor visible through her shoulders. When Alex turned, the room was empty.

“You see her?” he asked.

“I see an office and an open book,” Maya said. “Tell me what you see.”

Maya compared the ledger with her permit copies. “These names match the public death records. That’s verifiable. The earlier entries match Reyes’s cold-case summaries, too.”

At the bottom of the 2023 page, Alex found his name beside “DELIVERY NOT YET ACCEPTED.” Below it was Maya’s: “WITNESS—INTERVIEW PENDING.” The letters were pressed so deeply into the paper that the next page held their impression.

“I never wrote this,” Maya said.

“I know.”

She checked the ledger’s spine and found a pocket stitched into the binding. Inside lay a thin slip of tracing paper. The lines matched the floor plan she had brought, except for one narrow room beside the west stairwell. Its label had been rubbed away. Only the number remained: 17.

“A room, not a floor,” Maya said. “That could be the missing west lobby—or a storage space. I’ll compare it with the original permits before we decide.”

In the window, Evelyn lifted one hand and pointed toward the blank margin beside the 1927 entries. Alex leaned closer. A new line had appeared in the dust on the glass: “Ask who opened the door.”

Maya turned at the sound of his breath. The glass was clear to her. Alex looked back at the ledger. Beside the 1927 entry, someone had penciled a time: 11:17 p.m.

Maya photographed the page. “I can verify the room number,” she said. “I can’t verify what you just saw.”

Alex kept his eyes on the penciled time. “Then we find out who opened the door.”
